summary: Describes the architecture for SPIRITS services, which start in the telephone network and need to interact with the Internet. It explains how the two worlds are connected.

plainLanguage.summary: A SPIRITS service starts in the telephone network and needs the Internet to finish the job, such as showing a subscriber on a dial-up line that a call is waiting. This memo names the seven pieces such a system is built from and the five interfaces that connect them, so that equipment from different suppliers can work together.

subtitle: How a phone call can ask the Internet to do things on the subscriber's behalf, and the parts that make it work.

tldr.problem: Services that start in the telephone network and need the Internet, such as telling a subscriber on a dial-up line that a call is waiting, had no agreed set of components and interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines seven entities, among them the Service Control Function, the SPIRITS Client, the SPIRITS Gateway, the SPIRITS Server and the PINT Client and Server, and five interfaces labelled A to E that connect them.
tldr.outcome: The security section names interface B as the one that crosses the public Internet and is therefore the most exposed. The memo is Informational, and leaves the protocol and security detail to RFC 2848 and a companion requirements document.

facts.label: Example services
facts.value: Internet Call Waiting, Internet Caller-ID Delivery, Internet Call Forwarding

today: RFC 3136 is an Informational memo describing the SPIRITS architecture, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It names the components and the five interfaces, and points to RFC 2848 and a companion SPIRITS Protocol Requirements document for the protocol and security detail. It is read with RFC 2848 and with the survey of real implementations in RFC 2995.

sections.title: SPIRITS Services and the Architecture
sections.content:
The memo describes the architecture for supporting SPIRITS services, which are those originating in the PSTN, the Public Switched Telephone Network, and necessitating the interactions between the PSTN and the Internet. Internet Call Waiting, Internet Caller-ID Delivery and Internet Call Forwarding are given as examples of SPIRITS services. Specifically, it defines the components constituting the architecture and the interfaces between the components.

The rest of the document is organised as follows: Section 2 describes example SPIRITS services from the end-user point of view, Section 3 describes the SPIRITS architecture, Section 4 contains security considerations, and the Appendix contains the figure of the architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is a parts list. It names what each component does and which component talks to which, so that a switch, a gateway and a program on the subscriber's computer can be bought from different suppliers and still work together.

sections.title: Three Example Services
sections.content:
Three services are described from the end user's point of view, under three assumptions. Service subscription or cancellation is a separate process and may be done over the telephone, via postal mail, or over the Web. The subscriber's IP host, for example a PC, is loaded with the software needed to realise the service, including a Personal Identification Number and the IP addresses of the SPIRITS servers, and that software may be sent by postal mail or downloaded from the Web. The subscriber activates a service by an act of service session registration, which can take place any time after they are connected to the Internet, and may specify the life span of the session; as soon as the session ends the service is deactivated, and the subscriber should also be able to deactivate it at any time during the session.

For certain services, such as call waiting or caller-ID delivery, the assumption is that the service subscriber has a single telephone line and a PC connected to the Internet through that line. Only under this assumption do these services make sense. In other services, such as a Web-based call centre in which a call centre assistant could redirect or reject a call presented in a pop-up window, the assumption may be unnecessary or even inapplicable.

Internet call waiting enables a subscriber engaged in an Internet dial-up session to be notified of an incoming call to the very same telephone line that is being used for the Internet connection, to specify the desirable treatment of the call, and to have the call handled as specified. The ways of handling the waiting call include accepting it over the PSTN by terminating the Internet connection, in which case switching cannot be done immediately and the caller may hear an opening announcement followed by the ringing tone; forwarding it to another telephone number, where the subscriber stays connected and the caller hears an announcement indicating the call is being forwarded before being connected to the new destination; accepting it by voice over IP, although the proposed architecture does not reflect this feature; redirecting it to voice mail, with the caller hearing an invitation to leave a message; playing a pre-recorded message to the calling party and disconnecting the call; and rejecting it, with the caller hearing an announcement rejecting the call.

The subscriber may specify the call treatment on the fly when notified of an incoming call, or specify in advance a general treatment for all calls, such as redirection to voice mail, or treatments tailored to the origination numbers. When a call comes in under a rule, the subscriber is not presented with the call but can afterwards examine the treatment and outcome of the call from the log kept for all calls processed during the service, which typically records the incoming call date and time, the calling party number, the calling party name and the call disposition.

Internet caller-ID delivery allows the subscriber to see the caller's number or name or both while being connected to the Internet. Where the subscriber has only one telephone line and is using that line for the Internet connection, the service is a subset of call waiting and follows the description above; otherwise the subscriber's IP host serves as an auxiliary device of the telephone to which the call is first sent. Internet call forwarding allows the subscriber to forward an incoming call to another telephone number while being connected to the Internet, and follows the same rule about the IP host acting as an auxiliary device of the telephone.
sections.plainLanguage: The subscriber registers a session, the phone calls in, the computer shows a box, and the subscriber decides what happens. The three example services differ only in what the subscriber can see and do: see who is calling, or forward the call elsewhere.

sections.title: The Components
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the Appendix depicts the SPIRITS architecture, which includes the following entities.

The Service Control Function executes service logic, interacts with the entities in the IP domain, such as the SPIRITS Gateway and the PINT Server, through the SPIRITS Client, and instructs the switches on how to complete a call. Physically, the Service Control Function may be located in either stand-alone general-purpose computers called Service Control Points, or in specialized pieces of equipment called Service Nodes.

The Service Switching Function normally resides in a switch and is responsible for the recognition of Intelligent Network triggers and interactions with the Service Control Function.

The SPIRITS Client is responsible for receiving PSTN requests from the Service Control Function as well as sending responses back. It may be co-located with the Service Control Function. If not, it communicates with the Service Control Function over the D interface.

The PINT Server receives PINT requests from the PINT Client and relays them to the PSTN for execution over the E interface. The SPIRITS Gateway is co-located with the PINT Server, or the PINT Gateway, or both when they are co-located as assumed here for simplicity, and serves as an intermediary between the SPIRITS Server and the SPIRITS Client via the B and C interfaces respectively.

The PINT Client resides in the subscriber's IP host and is responsible for initiating PINT requests, which are sent to the PINT Server over the A interface. The SPIRITS Server terminates PSTN requests and is responsible for all interactions, such as incoming call notification and relaying the call treatment, between the subscriber and the SPIRITS Gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: Seven pieces do the work. The switch notices something about the call. A control function decides what to do about it and asks the Internet side. A gateway carries that request to the subscriber's computer and brings the answer back. On the subscriber's own machine a small program starts and ends the sessions.

sections.title: The Five Interfaces
sections.content:
Interface A is used for sending PINT requests to the PINT Server. Its principal use is for service session registration and, as a result, activation of a SPIRITS service. In addition, this interface may be used for service subscription.

Interface B serves two main purposes: to notify the subscriber of incoming calls, together with the calling number and name if available, and to send to the SPIRITS Gateway the subscriber's choice of call disposition specified on the fly.

Interface C is used for communications between the SPIRITS Client and the SPIRITS Gateway. The SPIRITS Gateway may in turn communicate with the SPIRITS Server, or may act as a virtual server, terminating the requests without sending them down to the SPIRITS Server.

Interface D is for communications between the SPIRITS Client and the Service Control Function. From the control function to the SPIRITS Client, the parameters associated with the applicable Intelligent Network triggers are sent. From the SPIRITS Client to the control function, the subscriber's call disposition is sent. The control function then transforms the user's disposition into appropriate actions, such as playing an announcement to the caller and resuming the suspended call processing in the switching point.

Interface E is for sending PINT requests to the Service Control Function for execution. In the appendix figure, the telephone network side shows the Service Switching Function talking to the Service Control Function over INAP and SS7, with the subscriber's telephone line running to the switching function.
sections.plainLanguage: Each interface has one job. A is for starting a session. B carries the alert to the subscriber and the answer back. C is the link between the telephone network side and the gateway. D carries the alert and the answer inside the telephone network side. E asks the control function to carry out a request.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As Figure 1 demonstrates, there are two distinct communications interfaces, B and C. The B interface is, in general, across the public Internet and is thus most vulnerable to security attacks resulting in theft or denial of service. The C interface, on the other hand, is likely to be implemented across a service provider's intranet, where the security measures should be applied at the discretion of the service provider. Even then, because at least one IP host, the PINT gateway, is connected to the Internet, special measures, such as the installation of firewalls, although this particular measure alone may be insufficient, need to be taken to protect interface C and the rest of the network from security attacks.

The assumption that the PINT Client and the SPIRITS Server are co-located dictates that the security considerations for the A and B interfaces are exactly the same. Detailed security requirements and solutions for interface A, and consequently B, can be found in RFC 2848. In addition, security requirements are listed in the companion SPIRITS Protocol Requirements document.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the traffic runs inside the telephone company's own network and can be protected as that operator sees fit. The link to the subscriber's computer crosses the public Internet, so that is the link that needs the most care, and the rules for it are in RFC 2848.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN ENTITIES OF THE SPIRITS ARCHITECTURE

items.title: Service Control Function
items.text: Executes the service logic and instructs the switches how to complete a call.

items.title: Service Switching Function
items.text: Lives in the switch, recognises the triggers and interacts with the control function.

items.title: SPIRITS Client
items.text: Receives the requests from the control function and sends the responses back.

items.title: PINT Server
items.text: Receives PINT requests from the PINT client and relays them to the telephone network.

items.title: SPIRITS Gateway
items.text: Sits between the SPIRITS server and the SPIRITS client.

items.title: PINT Client
items.text: Runs in the subscriber's host and initiates the PINT requests.

items.title: SPIRITS Server
items.text: Terminates PSTN requests and handles the interaction with the subscriber.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH OF THE FIVE INTERFACES CARRIES

cells: Service session registration and activation, and possibly service subscription
Notifying the subscriber of an incoming call and sending the call disposition
Communications between the client and the gateway
SPIRITS Client and Service Control Function
The trigger parameters out, and the subscriber's call disposition back
PINT Server and Service Control Function
Sending PINT requests to the control function for execution

viz.caption: THE INCOMING CALL PATH, ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC

messages.label: Trigger
messages.note: The switching function recognises an Intelligent Network trigger and reports it to the control function.

messages.label: Interface D
messages.note: The control function sends the parameters of the trigger to the SPIRITS client.

messages.label: Interface C
messages.note: The client relays the request to the SPIRITS gateway.

messages.label: Interface B
messages.note: The gateway notifies the subscriber's host of the incoming call, with the calling number and name if available.

messages.label: Call disposition
messages.note: The subscriber chooses what to do with the call and the choice is sent back.

messages.label: Interface C
messages.note: The gateway relays the disposition to the SPIRITS client.

messages.label: Interface D
messages.note: The client sends the subscriber's disposition to the control function.

messages.label: Action
messages.note: The control function turns the disposition into an action, such as an announcement to the caller.
